items.prompt: Choose the correct ending. If you heat ice, ___

options.text: it froze.
options.why: Froze is the past tense of freeze, the opposite of melting.

options.text: it would have melted.
options.why: This is for a past situation that did not happen.

options.text: it melts.
it melting.
options.why: Melting needs a helping verb, so this is not a complete sentence.

hints: This sentence is about something that is always true.
For facts that are always true, both parts of the sentence use the present tense.
Ask: what always happens to ice when it is heated?
items.explanation: If you heat ice, it melts. This is always true, so both clauses are in the present tense.

items.prompt: Write one word to complete the sentence. If it rains tomorrow, we ___ stay at home.
hints: The sentence is about something that could really happen tomorrow.
The if part is in the present tense. The result part talks about the future.
Which modal verb do we use for the future?
items.explanation: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home. For a real possibility in the future, use if with the present tense and will in the result.

items.prompt: Which sentence talks about something imaginary?

options.text: If I had wings, I would fly to school.
If it is sunny, we will go to the beach.
options.why: This is a real possibility.

options.text: If you press this button, the light comes on.
options.why: This is a fact that is always true.

options.text: If the bus is late, we will walk.
options.why: This could really happen.

hints: Imaginary means it cannot really happen, or is very unlikely.
Imaginary conditions use the past tense after if and would in the result.
Ask of each sentence: could this really happen?
items.explanation: People do not have wings, so this is imaginary. It uses had after if and would in the result.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to make a conditional sentence.
hints: Look for the word with a capital letter and the word with a full stop.
The if clause comes first, and it ends with a comma.
Start with If, then say who does the action.
items.explanation: If you water the plant, it will grow. The if clause comes first, then a comma, then the result.

items.prompt: Match each if clause to the ending that fits best.
pairs: If you mix red and yellow,
I will give him your message.
I would fly over the volcano.
we would have caught the train.
hints: Each if clause needs a result in the matching tense.
Present goes with present or will. Past goes with would. Had left goes with would have.
Start with If you mix red and yellow. Is that always true?
items.explanation: Facts use the present tense, real future possibilities use will, imaginary situations use would, and past situations that did not happen use would have.

items.prompt: Write the correct form of be. If I ___ you, I would wear a coat.
hints: This is an imaginary situation: I cannot really be you.
In imaginary if sentences, formal English uses a special form of be.
It is the same form you would use with they or we in the past.
items.explanation: In imaginary situations, we say If I were you. This is how we give advice politely.

items.prompt: Complete the sentence. If Pak Budi had checked the weather, he ___ his umbrella.

options.text: will take
options.why: Will take is for real future possibilities.

options.text: would take
options.why: This is for imaginary present situations. Had checked tells us it is about the past.

options.text: would have taken
takes
options.why: Takes is the present tense.

hints: Had checked tells us the sentence is about the past.
For a past situation that did not happen, the result uses would have and a past participle.
Did Pak Budi check the weather? Then did he take his umbrella?
items.explanation: He did not check the weather, so he did not take his umbrella. Past situations that did not happen use had in the if clause and would have in the result.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences that are correct.

options.text: If the road floods, the school will close.
If I would have known, I would have helped.
options.why: After if, use had known, not would have known.

options.text: If she had studied, she would have passed.
If you will mix blue and yellow, you get green.
options.why: For a fact, use the present tense after if: If you mix.

options.text: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

hints: Check the verb straight after if or unless in each sentence.
Would and will do not usually come straight after if.
Start with the sentence about the road. Is it a real possibility with the right tenses?
items.explanation: The correct sentences use the present after if for real possibilities, and had studied with would have passed for the past.

items.prompt: What does this sentence tell us? If we had planted the seeds in March, we would have had tomatoes by now.

options.text: They planted the seeds in March and have tomatoes now.
options.why: Had planted in an if clause means it did not happen.

options.text: They will plant the seeds next March.
options.why: The sentence is about the past, not the future.

options.text: They do not like tomatoes.
options.why: The sentence does not tell us what they like.

options.text: They did not plant the seeds in March, so they have no tomatoes yet.

hints: This kind of conditional talks about the past.
If clauses with had describe something that did not happen.
Ask: did they plant the seeds in March?
items.explanation: The sentence imagines a different past. They did not plant the seeds in March, so they do not have tomatoes yet.

items.prompt: Which sentence means the same as this one? You won’t pass the test unless you revise.

options.text: If you revise, you won’t pass the test.
options.why: This means revising would stop you passing.

options.text: If you don’t revise, you won’t pass the test.
You will pass the test if you don’t revise.
options.why: This means the opposite.

options.text: Unless you don’t revise, you will pass the test.
options.why: This double negative makes the meaning confusing.

hints: Unless means if not.
Replace unless with if not and see what the sentence becomes.
Start with: You won’t pass the test if you...
items.explanation: Unless means if not, so the sentence means: If you don’t revise, you won’t pass the test.

items.prompt: Choose the best ending. If you cool water to 0 degrees Celsius, ___
hints: This sentence is a scientific fact.
Facts use the present tense on both sides.
Both halves use the present simple.
items.explanation: The zero conditional is used for facts. Both clauses use the present simple: If you cool water, it freezes.

options.text: it froze.
options.why: This sentence is about a fact that is always true, so it needs the present tense.

options.text: it would freeze.
options.why: Would is for imaginary situations. This is a fact.

options.text: it freezes.
it will froze.
options.why: Will is never followed by a past form.

items.prompt: If the bell rings, the pupils ___ outside. If I won a prize, I ___ share it with my class.
hints: The first sentence is about something that always happens.
The second sentence is about something imaginary.
Imaginary if sentences use a past verb in the if clause and would in the other half.
items.explanation: The first is a zero conditional, so go. The second is a second conditional, so I would share.

items.prompt: Put the cards in order to make a sentence about an imaginary situation.
hints: Start with the if clause.
The if clause uses a past form, even though it is about now.
Put the comma after taller.
items.explanation: The second conditional uses a past verb in the if clause and would in the other half.
items.answer: If I were taller, I would play basketball.

items.prompt: Write the correct form of the verb. If Amara ___ (finish) early, she will help us.
hints: This sentence is about a real possibility.
The if clause uses the present simple.
Amara is she, so the verb needs an -s.
items.explanation: In a first conditional the if clause uses the present simple: If Amara finishes early.

items.prompt: Put the cards in order to make a conditional sentence.
hints: The if clause comes first and ends with a comma.
The result comes second.
Start with If it.
items.explanation: If it is sunny tomorrow, we will go to the beach. The if clause comes before the comma and the result comes after.

items.prompt: Which sentence is about a real possibility in the future?
hints: Real possibilities in the future use will in the result.
The if clause uses the present simple.
Look for is open and will buy.
items.explanation: The first conditional talks about real possibilities. The if clause is present and the result uses will.

options.text: If the shop were open, I would buy some bread.
options.why: This is about an imaginary situation, not a real possibility.

options.text: If the shop had been open, I would have bought some bread.
options.why: This is about the past and did not happen.

options.text: If you heat butter, it melts.
options.why: This is a fact that is always true.

options.text: If the shop is open, I will buy some bread.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences by type of conditional.
hints: Look at the verb in the if clause.
Zero and first use the present. Second uses a past form.
Zero conditionals do not have will or would.
items.explanation: Zero conditionals are facts. First conditionals use will for likely results. Second conditionals use would for imaginary situations.

items.text: If you freeze water, it becomes ice.
If you press the bell, it rings.
If it rains, we will stay in.
If you hurry, you will catch it.
If I were a bird, I would fly.
If I had a boat, I would sail.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the correct verb forms?
hints: Check the if clause first.
First conditionals use the present simple after if.
The result then uses will.
items.explanation: First conditional: If plus present simple, then will plus the base verb.

options.text: If she studies, she will pass.
If she will study, she will pass.
options.why: Will does not go in the if clause of a first conditional.

options.text: If she studied, she will pass.
options.why: The two halves do not match. After a past if clause use would.

options.text: If she study, she would pass.
options.why: Study should be studies with she, or studied for an imaginary sentence.

items.prompt: Rewrite using unless. If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus. You will miss the bus ___ you hurry.
hints: Unless means if not.
You will miss the bus if you do not hurry.
One word goes in the gap.
items.explanation: Unless means if not, so the two sentences mean the same.

items.prompt: The picnic was cancelled because it rained. Which sentence says this using a conditional?
hints: The picnic is already over, so the sentence is about the past.
A past situation that did not happen uses had plus a past participle.
The result uses would have plus a past participle.
items.explanation: The third conditional is for past situations that did not happen: If it had not rained, the picnic would have gone ahead.

options.text: If it does not rain, the picnic will go ahead.
options.why: This is about the future, but the rain has already happened.

options.text: If it had not rained, the picnic would have gone ahead.
If it did not rain, the picnic would go ahead.
options.why: This is about an imaginary present, but the sentence is about the past.

options.text: If it rains, the picnic would have been cancelled.
options.why: The verb forms do not match.

items.prompt: Rani did not eat breakfast, so she is hungry now. Which sentence matches this?
hints: The cause is in the past and the result is now.
The if clause is about the past, so use had plus a past participle.
The result clause is about now, so use would plus the base verb.
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional: If plus past perfect, then would plus the base verb.

options.text: If Rani ate breakfast, she would not have been hungry now.
options.why: The verb forms are the wrong way round for a past cause and a present result.

options.text: If Rani eats breakfast, she will not be hungry now.
options.why: This is a real future possibility, but the breakfast time has passed.

options.text: If Rani had eaten breakfast, she would not be hungry now.
If Rani would have eaten breakfast, she would not be hungry now.
options.why: Would have does not go in the if clause.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences with correct verb forms.
hints: Check the verb in each if clause.
Would and will do not normally go straight after if.
Look for the three matching pairs: past and would, present and present, had and would have.
items.explanation: The correct sentences match their verb forms. The wrong ones put would or will in the if clause or use the wrong form after would.

options.text: If I were you, I would apologise.
If the water boils, it turns to steam.
If I had known, I would have told you.
If he would come, we would start.
options.why: Would does not go in the if clause here.

options.text: If it will rain, we stay in.
options.why: Will does not go in the if clause, and the result needs will.

options.text: If she had gone, she would saw him.
options.why: After would the verb must be the base form: would have seen.

items.prompt: Complete the sentence. If I ___ known you were ill, I ___ have visited you.
hints: The speaker did not know, so this is about the past.
The if clause uses had plus a past participle.
The result clause uses would have.
items.explanation: Third conditional: If I had known, I would have visited.

items.prompt: Which sentence means the same as this one? If Hadi had not missed the bus, he would not have been late.
hints: A third conditional describes the opposite of what really happened.
Reverse each part: not missed becomes missed.
The bus came first, then the lateness.
items.explanation: The third conditional shows the opposite of the facts. In fact Hadi missed the bus and was late.

options.text: Hadi caught the bus, but he was late.
options.why: The sentence says he missed the bus, so he did not catch it.

options.text: Hadi missed the bus, so he was late.
Hadi was late, so he missed the bus.
options.why: This has the cause and result the wrong way round.

options.text: Hadi did not miss the bus, so he was late.
options.why: He did miss the bus. The if sentence is about something that did not happen.
